notes.meaning: Ahaz became king of Judah while Pekah was ruling over the northern kingdom of Israel. Ahaz had a godly father named Jotham, but he did not follow his father's good example. This note connects Judah's history to Israel during a time of great danger and looming war.

Ahaz took the throne at age twenty and ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. Even though King David was his ancestor, Ahaz refused to follow David's faithful walk with God. Growing up in a godly home does not guarantee that a child will love the Lord.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars and ancient translations read twenty-five instead of twenty for Ahaz's age, because starting at twenty would mean he fathered Hezekiah when he was only eleven.

notes.meaning: Ahaz copied the wicked habits of Israel's northern kings and turned to vile idolatry. He even sacrificed his own son in the fire to the pagan idol Molech. This was the first time a king of Judah took part in the horrific Canaanite practice of child sacrifice.

Ahaz offered sacrifices and burned incense at local pagan shrines, on hilltops, and under shaded trees. While earlier kings merely tolerated these high places, Ahaz personally participated in their corrupt rites. He chose to follow his own religious tastes rather than God's law.

The kings of Aram and Israel formed an alliance and marched against Jerusalem to dethrone Ahaz. They surrounded the city, but their siege failed because God protected the royal family of David. Even when Judah had an unfaithful king, the Lord kept His ancient covenant promises.

During the war, King Rezin of Aram seized the vital port city of Elath on the Red Sea. He drove out the people of Judah, and people allied with him settled there permanently. When God's people turn away from Him, they often lose blessings they once enjoyed.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars and ancient translations suggest the text originally meant Edom rather than Aram, meaning Rezin helped the Edomites regain control of Elath from Judah.

notes.meaning: Instead of seeking help from the Lord, Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser, the king of Assyria. He offered to become the pagan king's humble servant and son if Assyria would rescue him. Ahaz chose to put his trust in a cruel foreign power rather than the living God.

To pay for Assyria's military aid, Ahaz gathered the gold and silver from the temple and the royal palace. He handed over these dedicated treasures as a bribe to a heathen emperor. Using holy things to buy worldly protection only leads to greater trouble.

The king of Assyria accepted the bribe and attacked the Syrian capital of Damascus. He captured the city, carried its citizens away into exile, and put King Rezin to death. This fulfilled God's earlier prophecy through Amos, yet it brought Judah under Assyrian control.

Ahaz traveled to Damascus to pay homage to the Assyrian king after the victory. While there, he admired an ornate pagan altar and sent detailed drawings of it back to Jerusalem. He ordered Uriah the priest to build an exact copy for God's temple.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some historians suggest the altar Ahaz saw was an Assyrian military altar, and that he made a copy to honor his new Assyrian master.

notes.meaning: Uriah the chief priest followed the king's orders without any recorded question or protest. He finished building the foreign-styled altar before Ahaz returned home to Jerusalem. Religious leaders fail their duty when they obey sinful commands instead of guarding God's house.

When Ahaz returned to Jerusalem, he inspected the new altar and went up to offer sacrifices on it. By doing this, he improperly took on the sacred duties of a priest. Human pride often leads people to worship however they please instead of how God commands.

Ahaz presented burnt offerings, grain offerings, drink offerings, and peace offerings on the new altar. He also sprinkled the sacrificial blood across it, copying the rituals of God's law for an unauthorized altar. Outward ceremonies mean nothing to God when they disobey His Word.

The original bronze altar made by Solomon stood right in front of the temple sanctuary. Ahaz moved it out of the way to an obscure spot on the north side, giving the primary place of honor to his new altar. He pushed God's appointed worship aside to make room for his own ideas.

Ahaz commanded Uriah to offer all regular morning, evening, and royal sacrifices on the new altar. He set aside the original bronze altar for his own private use to seek guidance or consider later. In doing so, he officially replaced God's holy altar with a man-made substitute.

Uriah the priest followed every command that King Ahaz gave him. Instead of rebuking the king and defending God's ordinances, he helped establish the corrupt worship. It is a tragedy when ministers please earthly rulers instead of the Lord.

Ahaz damaged the sacred temple furnishings by cutting the bronze panels off the movable washstands and taking off their basins. He also removed the large bronze basin called the Sea from the twelve bronze oxen and set it on a plain stone base. He likely did this to strip away valuable metal to pay tribute to Assyria.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some commentators suggest Ahaz damaged these ornate furnishings out of sheer financial necessity, driven to strip the temple bronze to meet repeated Assyrian demands.

notes.meaning: Ahaz took down the covered shelter used at the temple on the Sabbath and closed the royal walkway into the Lord's house. He did this to appease or accommodate the king of Assyria, showing disrespect for the Sabbath day. Those who abandon God's house to please worldly rulers walk toward their own ruin.

The writer notes that the rest of the events of Ahaz's reign were written down in the royal records of Judah. These official chronicles kept a full record of his life and choices. God sees and remembers every action of earthly rulers.

Ahaz died at age thirty-six and was buried in the City of David, but not in the royal tombs of the kings. His godly son Hezekiah became king in his place and later worked to restore true worship. Even after seasons of deep darkness, God can raise up faithful leaders to bring renewal.
